stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of low mood, anhedonia, poor concentration, reduced energy, and early morning wakening. She has no prior psychiatric history. PHQ-9 score is 16. She is medically well and takes no regular medications. According to NICE guidelines, what is the most appropriate first-line management?
options: High-intensity psychological therapy (CBT or IPT) alone
Sertraline 50mg daily plus low-intensity psychosocial intervention
Referral to crisis team for urgent assessment
distractors_rationale: Watchful waiting is for subthreshold/mild depression (PHQ-9 < 10). A PHQ-9 of 16 indicates moderate depression, which requires active treatment.

High-intensity psychological therapy alone is appropriate for moderate depression when the patient declines medication, but NICE recommends offering antidepressant medication OR high-intensity psychological therapy. The combination of medication PLUS low-intensity psychosocial intervention (guided self-help, physical activity programme) is most appropriate as first-line for moderate depression.

CORRECT. NICE CG90 (updated) recommends for moderate depression: offer antidepressant medication OR a high-intensity psychological intervention. Additionally, a low-intensity psychosocial intervention (guided self-help, behavioural activation, exercise programme) should be offered alongside. Sertraline is the first-line SSRI due to favourable side-effect profile and safety in overdose.

Venlafaxine is not first-line for moderate depression. NICE recommends SSRIs (sertraline, fluoxetine, citalopram) as first-line. Venlafaxine (SNRI) is reserved for second-line or where an SSRI has failed, due to higher side-effect burden and toxicity in overdose.
Crisis team referral is for acute risk (suicidality, self-harm, psychotic depression). There is no indication of immediate risk in this presentation.
teaching_point: NICE stepped care for depression: For moderate depression (PHQ-9 10-19), offer an antidepressant (SSRI first-line — sertraline preferred) OR high-intensity psychological therapy (CBT/IPT). A low-intensity psychosocial intervention (guided self-help, exercise) should be offered alongside. Sertraline is first-line SSRI due to good tolerability and safety in overdose. Fluoxetine has longest half-life (least discontinuation syndrome) but more initial activation. Citalopram carries QTc prolongation risk >40mg.
source: NICE CG90: Depression in adults (updated)

stem: A 28-year-old man with a history of epilepsy (well-controlled on lamotrigine) presents with a 5-week history of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, and suicidal ideation without plan. PHQ-9 is 18. Which antidepressant is the safest first-line choice given his epilepsy?
distractors_rationale: Sertraline is generally safe in epilepsy but carries a slightly increased risk of seizures at higher doses (RR ~1.5). SSRIs as a class are not contraindicated, but mirtazapine has the lowest seizure risk of all antidepressants.

CORRECT. Mirtazapine is the safest antidepressant in patients with epilepsy. It has the lowest seizure risk of all antidepressants (RR ~0.5-1.0 compared to placebo). It acts on presynaptic α2-adrenoceptors and 5-HT2/5-HT3 receptors. Additionally, it has beneficial effects on sleep and appetite — useful in depressed patients with insomnia and weight loss.

Tricyclic antidepressants, especially amitriptyline, are PROCONVULSANT. They lower the seizure threshold and are relatively contraindicated in epilepsy. Amitriptyline is associated with dose-dependent seizure risk (RR ~2-4).
Venlafaxine (SNRI) at higher doses (>150mg) is associated with increased seizure risk and is also more dangerous in overdose (cardiotoxicity, serotonin syndrome). Not first-line in epilepsy.

Bupropion is absolutely contraindicated in epilepsy. It is a noradrenaline-dopamine reuptake inhibitor that significantly lowers the seizure threshold. Seizure risk is dose-dependent (~0.4% at 300mg, ~4% at 450mg).
teaching_point: Antidepressant choice in epilepsy: Mirtazapine (NaSSA) has the lowest seizure risk, making it the safest choice. SSRIs (sertraline, fluoxetine, citalopram) are generally safe but carry a small increased risk at high doses. TCAs are proconvulsant (amitriptyline highest risk). Bupropion is contraindicated in epilepsy. Always check the BNF/NICE guidelines for antidepressant prescribing in patients with comorbid physical illness.
source: BNF; NICE CG90; Mula M, Sander JW (2013) Antidepressants in epilepsy

stem: A 52-year-old man is referred with a 6-month history of low mood, poor concentration, reduced energy, and anhedonia. He has insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes with HbA1c of 78 mmol/mol. PHQ-9 is 17. He was previously tried on sertraline 100mg daily for 8 weeks with no improvement. What is the most appropriate next-step antidepressant?
distractors_rationale: Sertraline 100mg is already at a therapeutic dose after 8 weeks with no response. The maximum licensed dose is 200mg, but increasing further is not recommended as first step after non-response — switching or augmenting is preferred. However, in this patient with diabetes, mirtazapine is a better option.

Switching to another SSRI (fluoxetine) is a reasonable option after SSRI failure (class switching), but in this patient with poorly controlled diabetes and weight loss, mirtazapine's weight gain and improved glycaemic control may be beneficial.

CORRECT. Mirtazapine is a good choice in depression comorbid with diabetes because: (1) it can improve appetite and weight in patients with anorexia associated with depression; (2) it may improve glycaemic control through weight gain; (3) it is effective in depression; (4) it has a favourable side-effect profile regarding seizures and sexual dysfunction. After failure of one SSRI at an adequate dose for 8 weeks, NICE recommends switching to an alternative antidepressant (different class).

Venlafaxine is an option after SSRI failure, but it requires monitoring of BP (hypertension risk), can worsen glycaemic control, and is more dangerous in overdose. Mirtazapine is a better choice in this specific patient.
Augmentation is a strategy after failure of two or more antidepressants (treatment-resistant depression, TRD). This patient has only failed one SSRI, so switching is the preferred next step per NICE.
teaching_point: Management after first antidepressant failure: NICE recommends (1) check adherence, (2) check diagnosis (is it bipolar depression?), (3) consider switching to a different class (e.g., SSRI → NaSSA/SNRI). SSRIs can worsen glycaemic control in diabetes; mirtazapine is associated with weight gain which can paradoxically improve HbA1c in underweight patients but must be monitored in obesity. Mirtazapine also has the lowest sexual dysfunction rate of all antidepressants.
source: NICE CG90; NICE NG19: Diabetes in adults; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: According to the STAR*D trial, what is the cumulative remission rate after up to four sequential treatment steps for major depressive disorder?
distractors_rationale: 47% is the remission rate after Level 2 (switch/augment) only. The cumulative rate across all 4 levels is higher.

CORRECT. The STAR*D (Sequenced Treatment Alternatives to Relieve Depression) trial found cumulative remission rates of: Level 1 (citalopram) 36.8%, Level 2 (switch/augment) 30.6% of remaining, Level 3 13.7% of remaining, Level 4 13.0% of remaining. The overall cumulative remission rate across all 4 levels was approximately 67%.
53% does not correspond to any specific STAR*D outcome.
37% is the Level 1 (citalopram monotherapy) remission rate — not cumulative.
80% overestimates the cumulative rate. Even with aggressive treatment, approximately 33% of patients remain symptomatic after 4 treatment levels.
teaching_point: STAR*D (Rush et al., 2006) is the landmark pragmatic trial of treatment-resistant depression. Key findings: (1) Step 1 (citalopram) remission = 36.8%; (2) subsequent steps have diminishing returns; (3) cumulative remission after 4 steps = ~67%; (4) no significant difference between switch and augment strategies at any level; (5) approximately 1 in 3 patients remain depressed despite multiple adequate trials. The take-home for MRCPsych: citalopram was the index drug; sertraline, bupropion, venlafaxine were switch options; augmentation options included bupropion, buspirone, and T3.
source: Rush AJ et al. (2006) STAR*D. Am J Psychiatry; NICE CG90

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with low mood, poor appetite, and early morning wakening 4 weeks after an ischaemic stroke affecting his left middle cerebral artery territory. He has a past history of hypertension and a GI bleed 2 years ago requiring transfusion. Mental State Examination reveals depressive cognitions but no psychotic features. PHQ-9 is 15. Which antidepressant is the safest and most appropriate first-line choice?
distractors_rationale: Amitriptyline is a TCA with significant anticholinergic burden, sedation, and postural hypotension — risky in elderly post-stroke patients. It also has QTc prolongation risk. Not first-line.

Sertraline is an SSRI. While SSRIs are generally options for post-stroke depression, their association with GI bleeding (due to platelet serotonin depletion) is a relative contraindication here given the history of a significant GI bleed. The risk is elevated in elderly patients on NSAIDs or anticoagulants.

CORRECT. Nortriptyline is a TCA that is preferred in post-stroke depression because: (1) it has fewer anticholinergic effects than amitriptyline; (2) it has less postural hypotension than other TCAs; (3) it does not carry the GI bleeding risk associated with SSRIs; (4) in post-stroke depression, TCAs have evidence of efficacy from RCTs (e.g., Lipsey et al., 1984). Nortriptyline is the TCA of choice in elderly patients and those with cardiovascular comorbidity.

Citalopram is an SSRI with QTc prolongation risk at higher doses (>40mg, >20mg in over-65s). While safer than TCAs in most elderly patients, the GI bleed history means a TCA (nortriptyline) is preferable.
Phenelzine (MAOI) requires dietary restrictions and carries risk of hypertensive crisis. It is reserved for treatment-resistant cases only. Absolutely not first-line in any scenario.
teaching_point: Post-stroke depression affects approximately 30% of stroke survivors. Treatment choice must account for: (1) GI bleeding risk with SSRIs (platelet serotonin depletion); (2) cardiovascular side effects of TCAs; (3) drug interactions with antihypertensives and anticoagulants. Nortriptyline has the best evidence in post-stroke depression with the most favourable TCA side-effect profile. Sertraline can be used if no GI bleeding risk. NICE recommends SSRIs or TCAs for post-stroke depression based on individual patient factors.
source: NICE CG90; NICE NG128: Stroke rehabilitation; Lipsey JR et al. (1984) Nortriptyline in post-stroke depression; BNF

stem: According to the literature, approximately what proportion of patients with major depressive disorder will have a recurrence within 5-10 years after recovery from an index episode?
distractors_rationale: 20-30% underestimates recurrence. Even 40-50% is too low.
40-50% is closer but still below the actual figure reported in long-term follow-up studies.

CORRECT. Long-term outcome studies (e.g., Keller et al., 1992; Judd et al., 1998; the NIMH Collaborative Depression Study) consistently show that 60-75% of patients with MDD will experience at least one further episode within 5-10 years. The risk increases with each subsequent episode: after 1 episode ~50% recurrence, after 2 episodes ~70%, after 3+ episodes ~90%.
80-90% is the recurrence risk after 3 or more episodes, not after an index episode.
<10% is clearly wrong — MDD is a relapsing-remitting condition for the majority.
teaching_point: Recurrence in MDD: The natural history of MDD is characterised by high recurrence rates. After a first episode, the risk of recurrence is ~50% within 5 years. This rises to 70% after a second episode and 90% after a third. NICE recommends maintenance antidepressants for at least 2 years for patients at high risk of recurrence (those with 2+ episodes, severe episodes, or residual symptoms). The distinction between relapse (return of symptoms within 6 months of recovery — same episode) and recurrence (new episode after full recovery) is the Kupfer curve concept.
source: Keller MB et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1992; Judd LL et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1998; NICE CG90

stem: A 42-year-old woman with a history of recurrent major depressive disorder (two previous episodes) presents at 30 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She reports low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, and reduced energy over 6 weeks. PHQ-9 is 16. She had been stable on sertraline 100mg daily prior to pregnancy but stopped it at 6 weeks gestation after learning she was pregnant. She is now keen to restart medication. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Advise against restarting medication — refer for CBT instead
distractors_rationale: CBT alone would be appropriate for mild depression, but this is moderate depression (PHQ-9 16) with functional impairment. The risk of untreated depression in pregnancy (poor foetal growth, preterm birth, postnatal depression, impaired bonding) often outweighs the small risks of SSRIs.

CORRECT. Reinstating the same antidepressant that was previously effective at the same dose is the recommended approach. Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy due to extensive safety data and low placental passage. The BNF advises that SSRI use in pregnancy should be individualised; sertraline and fluoxetine have the largest safety database. The risk of relapse if antidepressants are stopped in pregnancy is 68-90%, compared to 26% in those who continue.

Fluoxetine has a long half-life (4-6 days, active metabolite 7-9 days) which is less desirable in pregnancy due to longer neonatal exposure and risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension (PPHN, absolute risk ~3/1000 vs 1/1000 background). Sertraline is preferred.
Mirtazapine has less safety data in pregnancy than sertraline. While not contraindicated, reinstating her previously effective treatment is more appropriate.
Nortriptyline is a TCA with a narrower therapeutic index and higher side-effect burden. It is not first-line when a previously effective SSRI is available.
teaching_point: Depression in pregnancy: The risk of relapse is high (68-90%) in women who discontinue antidepressants, with over half of relapses occurring in the first trimester. Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy due to: (1) extensive safety data; (2) low placental passage; (3) lowest PPHN risk. Paroxetine should be avoided (associated with cardiac defects). Fluoxetine carries slightly higher PPHN risk. Venlafaxine can cause neonatal withdrawal. The principles: use the lowest effective dose of the drug that worked previously; monotherapy preferred; avoid polypharmacy; consider baseline foetal ultrasound and neonatal adaptation syndrome monitoring.
source: NICE CG192: Antenatal and postnatal mental health; BNF; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Pregnancy

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder presents with low mood, anhedonia, irritability, and sleep disturbance of 3 weeks' duration. She has a history of recurrent self-harm (cutting) and three previous presentations to A&E with overdoses. PHQ-9 is 14. What is the most appropriate management according to NICE guidelines?
options: Admit to psychiatric ward for assessment
distractors_rationale: Antidepressants (SSRIs) are not recommended as first-line treatment for depression in patients with borderline personality disorder. NICE CG78 states that drug treatment should not be used specifically for BPD or for symptoms associated with BPD, including depression. Transient depressive symptoms in the context of BPD often resolve with psychological intervention.
Mirtazapine is similarly not recommended as first-line for depressive symptoms in BPD. Medication has a limited evidence base in this population and carries risk of overdose.

This is the correct answer. BPD and depression: Depressive symptoms in BPD can be difficult to distinguish from episodes of major depression. NICE is clear: drug treatment should NOT be used for BPD or for associated symptoms. The evidence does not support SSRIs for depressive symptoms in BPD. Psychological therapy is first-line. If depression is severe and persistent (>6 weeks) despite psychological therapy, a short-term trial of an SSRI may be considered, but should be agreed with the patient regarding limited evidence of benefit. Self-harm should be managed within a DBT framework.

This is the correct answer. BPD and depression: Depressive symptoms in BPD can be difficult to distinguish from episodes of major depression. NICE is clear: drug treatment should NOT be used for BPD or for associated symptoms. The evidence does not support SSRIs for depressive symptoms in BPD. Psychological therapy is first-line. If depression is severe and persistent (>6 weeks) despite psychological therapy, a short-term trial of an SSRI may be considered, but should be agreed with the patient regarding limited evidence of benefit. Self-harm should be managed within a DBT framework.

CORRECT. NICE CG78 recommends structured psychological therapy (specifically DBT, mentalisation-based therapy, or CBT) as first-line for people with BPD. For depressive symptoms that occur in the contex ptoms without acute risk of suicide (no current suicidal ideation or plan described). DBT can be provided in outpatient settings.
teaching_point: BPD and depression: Depressive symptoms in BPD can be difficult to distinguish from episodes of major depression. NICE is clear: drug treatment should NOT be used for BPD or for associated symptoms. The evidence does not support SSRIs for depressive symptoms in BPD. Psychological therapy is first-line. If depression is severe and persistent (>6 weeks) despite psychological therapy, a short-term trial of an SSRI may be considered, but should be agreed with the patient regarding limited evidence of benefit. Self-harm should be managed within a DBT framework.
source: NICE CG78: Borderline personality disorder; NICE CG90: Depression

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with severe depressive episode with psychotic features. He is convinced his internal organs are rotting and that he is responsible for causing a recent flood in his town. He has poor oral intake and is losing weight. His PHQ-9 is 24. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Fluoxetine 20mg daily augmented with olanzapine 5mg daily
Venlafaxine 225mg daily augmented with aripiprazole 5mg daily
distractors_rationale: CORRECT. For severe depression with psychotic features, NICE recommends combination therapy with an antidepressant and an antipsychotic. Fluoxetine + olanzapine is the most studied combination (also referred to as OFC — olanzapine-fluoxetine combination). Alternatively, amitriptyline alone or an SSRI with an antipsychotic are options. The combination of an antidepressant with an atypical antipsychotic is first-line pharmacological treatment for psychotic depression.

ECT is highly effective for psychotic depression (response rate 80-90%) and is recommended when there is a need for rapid response (e.g., poor oral intake, high suicide risk, catatonia). However, it is not first-line for psychotic depression unless there is urgency, treatment resistance, or patient preference after discussing options. NICE recommends ECT for severe depression with psychotic features when there is a need for rapid improvement or where pharmacological treatment has failed.

Amitriptyline 150mg alone is insufficient — psychotic depression requires an antipsychotic in combination. While amitriptyline has evidence as monotherapy for psychotic depression (unlike SSRIs alone), combined therapy is more effective.
SSRI alone is insufficient for psychotic depression. The psychotic component requires an antipsychotic. Antidepressant monotherapy has poor response rates (<30%) in delusional depression.

Venlafaxine + aripiprazole is a reasonable combination but is not the most studied or established first-line option. Fluoxetine + olanzapine has the strongest evidence base (including FDA approval for bipolar depression and psychotic depression).
teaching_point: Psychotic (delusional) depression: Characterised by depressive symptoms with mood-congruent delusions/hallucinations (e.g., nihilistic, guilty, somatic). Pharmacologically, it requires BOTH an antidepressant and an antipsychotic — neither alone is sufficient (response rates: combination ~80%, antidepressant alone ~30%, antipsychotic alone ~25%). ECT is highly effective (80-90% response) and should be considered early if the patient is refusing food/fluids, catatonic, or at high suicide risk. NICE recommends offering combination therapy (antidepressant + antipsychotic) as first-line or ECT.
source: NICE CG90; NICE TA136 (ECT); Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 74-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history presents with a 3-week history of low mood, tearfulness, and anxiety. She lives alone and has become increasingly socially withdrawn. MSE reveals depressive cognitions but no psychotic features. She has a history of atrial fibrillation (rate-controlled on bisoprolol), hypertension, and previous TIA. Her ECG shows QTc interval of 455ms. PHQ-9 is 15. What is the most appropriate antidepressant for this patient?
distractors_rationale: Citalopram carries a dose-related risk of QTc prolongation. The BNF advises maximum 20mg daily in over-65s and avoidance if QTc >450ms. This patient's QTc is 455ms, so citalopram is best avoided.
Sertraline has minimal QTc effect and is generally safe in elderly patients. However, mirtazapine offers additional advantages in this patient (see below). Sertraline is a reasonable alternative.

CORRECT. Mirtazapine is the best choice in this elderly patient because: (1) it has no QTc prolongation effect (safe in this patient's prolonged QTc); (2) it has minimal CYP450 interactions (unlikely to interact with bisoprolol or antihypertensives); (3) its sedative effects at 15mg can help with insomnia common in late-life depression; (4) it has appetite-stimulating effects useful in elderly patients with weight loss; (5) no postural hypotension (unlike TCAs); (6) no significant sexual dysfunction.

Nortriptyline is a TCA. Despite being the best-tolerated TCA, it still carries risk of postural hypotension and QTc prolongation. The TCA class has anticholinergic effects that can worsen cognition in elderly patients. Not first-choice here.

Fluoxetine has the longest half-life (4-6 days, active metabolite norfluoxetine 7-9 days), which is disadvantageous in elderly patients if side effects occur. It also has significant CYP2D6 inhibition potential (drug interactions). In elderly patients, a shorter half-life SSRI (sertraline) or mirtazapine is preferred.
teaching_point: Antidepressant choice in elderly with cardiovascular disease: Mirtazapine is often preferred because of its unique side-effect profile: (1) no QTc effect; (2) no CYP450 inhibition (fewer drug interactions with cardiac meds); (3) sedation aids sleep; (4) appetite stimulation aids nutrition; (5) minimal sexual dysfunction; (6) no hyponatraemia risk (lower than SSRIs). SSRIs carry hyponatraemia risk (SIADH) in elderly, QTc risk with citalopram, and interaction with warfarin/antiplatelets via platelet serotonin depletion. TCAs carry postural hypotension, anticholinergic, and QTc risks.
source: BNF; NICE CG90; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Taylor D, Carol Paton, Kapur S

stem: A 45-year-old man is referred with low mood, anhedonia, and poor concentration of 7 weeks' duration. He is known to have chronic kidney disease stage 4 (eGFR 22 ml/min/1.73m2, stable over 6 months). PHQ-9 is 16. He has no prior psychiatric history. Which antidepressant is safest and most appropriate as first-line?
distractors_rationale: Citalopram is not contraindicated in renal impairment, but its dose must be adjusted (max 20mg if eGFR <20). However, sertraline has a better safety margin — no dose adjustment required in renal impairment and no active metabolites that accumulate.
Amitriptyline is predominantly renally excreted and its active metabolites (nortriptyline) can accumulate in CKD, increasing anticholinergic and cardiotoxic risks. Avoid or use with extreme caution.
Duloxetine (SNRI) is contraindicated if eGFR <30 due to accumulation of conjugated metabolites. This patient's eGFR is 22, so duloxetine is contraindicated per BNF.

CORRECT. Sertraline is the safest SSRI in renal impairment because: (1) it is extensively metabolised in the liver to an inactive metabolite; (2) no dose adjustment is required in any degree of renal impairment; (3) it does not accumulate in CKD; (4) it has minimal effect on QTc; (5) it has no significant drug interactions with common renal medications. Sertraline is the first-line antidepressant in chronic kidney disease per Maudsley Guidelines.

Venlafaxine is predominantly eliminated renally and its active metabolite (O-desmethylvenlafaxine) accumulates in renal impairment. The BNF advises caution with dose adjustment or avoidance in severe renal impairment. Not first-line in CKD stage 4.
teaching_point: Antidepressant selection in chronic kidney disease: Sertraline is the safest SSRI in renal impairment (no dose adjustment needed). Fluoxetine and paroxetine also have favourable renal profiles. Duloxetine and venlafaxine (SNRIs) accumulate significantly in renal impairment (avoid if eGFR <30). TCAs accumulate active metabolites and increase cardiotoxicity risk. Citalopram is safe but requires dose adjustment (max 20mg if eGFR <20). Mirtazapine is also a good option (hepatic metabolism, no renal adjustment needed). Always check the BNF and Maudsley for specific dose guidance.
source: BNF; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; NICE CG90

stem: According to the NICE stepped-care model for depression, which intervention is most appropriate for a 22-year-old woman with subthreshold depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 score of 8) who has had symptoms for 3 weeks following a relationship breakup?
options: Watchful waiting with follow-up in 2 weeks
Referral for group exercise programme and guided self-help
distractors_rationale: Antidepressants are not recommended for subthreshold or mild depression (PHQ-9 <10) unless it persists after other interventions or has been present for >2 years (persistent subthreshold depression).
High-intensity psychological therapy is for moderate-severe depression, not first-line for subthreshold/mild symptoms.

Watchful waiting alone is appropriate for subthreshold depression that does not meet criteria for a depressive episode. However, NICE stepped care recommends offering low-intensity psychosocial interventions for persistent subthreshold depression (>2 weeks). Group exercise and guided self-help are low-intensity interventions.

CORRECT. For persistent subthreshold depressive symptoms (lasting >2 weeks) or mild depression, NICE recommends low-intensity psychosocial interventions. These include: (1) individual guided self-help based on CBT principles; (2) computerised CBT; (3) structured group physical activity programme; (4) group-based peer support. If these are declined or ineffective, consider high-intensity psychological therapy or medication.
Crisis team referral would only be indicated if there is acute risk (suicidality, self-harm, psychotic symptoms), which is not described here.
teaching_point: NICE stepped care for depression — Step 1: recognition and assessment, watchful waiting. Step 2 (persistent subthreshold/mild): low-intensity psychosocial interventions (guided self-help, computerised CBT, structured exercise, peer support). Step 3 (moderate-severe): antidepressant plus high-intensity psychological therapy. Step 4 (complex/severe/refractory/at risk): multidisciplinary team input including crisis teams, complex medication regimes, ECT. Key exam point: low-intensity interventions are for mild/persistent subthreshold depression, NOT medication.
source: NICE CG90: Depression in adults: recognition and management

stem: A 26-year-old woman who recently started taking fluoxetine 20mg daily for moderate depression reports feeling more agitated, anxious, and restless since starting the medication 5 days ago. She is concerned and considering stopping the medication. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop fluoxetine immediately and switch to mirtazapine
Reassure that this is a common transient side effect and advise continuing
Reduce dose to fluoxetine 10mg on alternate days
distractors_rationale: Switching after only 5 days is premature. Initial activation/agitation with SSRIs is a known, transient phenomenon that typically resolves within the first 1-2 weeks. Patients should be counselled about this at the time of prescribing.

CORRECT. Early-onset agitation, anxiety, and restlessness are common transient side effects of SSRIs, particularly fluoxetine (which has the most activating profile). This typically occurs in the first few days to 2 weeks and resolves spontaneously. Patients should be warned about this at initiation and encouraged to continue. If symptoms significantly worsen or new akathisia develops, review urgently.
Dose reduction is not indicated at this stage as the activation is a pharmacodynamic effect, not dose-dependent. The 20mg dose is appropriate.
PRN benzodiazepines can be used short-term (1-2 weeks) if agitation is severe, but they are not routinely recommended and carry dependence risk. Reassurance and support are first-line.
Admission is not indicated for mild transient SSRI side effects without suicidal ideation or severe akathisia.
teaching_point: SSRI side effects — initial activation: SSRIs (especially fluoxetine) can cause an initial transient increase in anxiety, agitation, and restlessness (sometimes called 'jitteriness syndrome'). This is thought to be due to initial serotonergic overstimulation before receptor desensitisation occurs. It typically resolves within 1-2 weeks. Patients MUST be warned about this at initiation. If severe or persistent, consider: (1) starting at a lower dose and titrating; (2) switching to a less activating SSRI (sertraline, citalopram) or mirtazapine. Rarely, it can herald serotonergic toxicity or bipolar switching. Always exclude akathisia.
source: BNF; NICE CG90; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 38-year-old woman with recurrent major depressive disorder has been on sertraline 100mg daily for 6 weeks with partial improvement (PHQ-9 reduced from 20 to 14). She reports significant fatigue, reduced energy, and poor motivation as her residual symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step?
distractors_rationale: Increasing the dose is reasonable (sertraline max 200mg) but the patient has some response already. However, for residual fatigue specifically, augmentation strategies targeting residual symptoms may be more targeted.

California rocket fuel (SSRI + mirtazapine) is a strategy for treatment-resistant depression but is more commonly used when there has been a poor response to SSRI alone. The patient has had partial response (PHQ-9 dropped from 20 to 14 — 30% reduction). This is not yet treatment-resistant.
Switch to venlafaxine is reasonable after SSRI partial response, but modafinil augmentation is specifically recommended for residual fatigue and has evidence in this context.

CORRECT. Modafinil augmentation of SSRIs has evidence for improving residual fatigue, sleepiness, and cognitive symptoms in partial responders to antidepressants. NICE acknowledges augmentation strategies for residual symptoms. Modafinil 100-200mg daily (off-label) is a recognised augmentation strategy for residual fatigue in MDD. However, it should be used cautiously due to risk of mania switching in bipolar disorder (ensure diagnosis is unipolar).

Aripiprazole augmentation is licensed for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) after failure of 1-2 adequate antidepressant trials. This patient has only had partial response to one trial — not yet TRD.
teaching_point: Residual symptoms in depression: Up to 50% of responders to antidepressant treatment have residual symptoms. Fatigue and cognitive symptoms are among the most common. Management strategies include: (1) optimise current dose; (2) switch to a different antidepressant; (3) targeted augmentation. Modafinil (off-label) has evidence for residual fatigue. Other options include bupropion augmentation (not available in UK), or switching to a more activating antidepressant (fluoxetine, venlafaxine). Note: 'California rocket fuel' (SSRI + mirtazapine) is effective for TRD but mirtazapine may worsen fatigue/sedation at low doses.
source: NICE CG90; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Am J Psychiatry 2007 (Fava et al.) modafinil augmentation

stem: Which of the following antidepressant discontinuation syndromes is most commonly associated with paroxetine compared to other SSRIs?
distractors_rationale: CORRECT. Paroxetine has the highest risk of discontinuation syndrome among all SSRIs (incidence ~30-50%). This is due to its short half-life (~21 hours) and absence of active metabolites. Symptoms include: dizziness, flu-like symptoms, nausea, headache, paraesthesias (electric shock sensations), insomnia, and vivid dreams. The syndrome typically occurs within 2-4 days of stopping or reducing the dose and can last 1-2 weeks. Fluoxetine has the lowest risk (half-life ~4-6 days, active metabolite norfluoxetine ~7-9 days).
Manic switch is a risk with all antidepressants in bipolar disorder, not specific to paroxetine or to discontinuation. It is more associated with TCAs and venlafaxine than SSRIs.
Weight gain and metabolic syndrome are common with paroxetine (more than other SSRIs) but these are treatment-emergent, not discontinuation effects.
QTc prolongation is associated with citalopram (>40mg), not specifically paroxetine.
Hepatic failure is not a known side effect of paroxetine.
teaching_point: Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome: Risk is proportional to half-life. Paroxetine (shortest SSRI half-life, no active metabolite) → highest risk. Venlafaxine (short half-life) → also high risk. Fluoxetine (longest half-life, active metabolite) → lowest risk. Sertraline (intermediate). Citalopram/escitalopram (intermediate). Management: (1) gradual taper (reduce by 10mg every 1-2 weeks for paroxetine); (2) if severe, reintroduce the antidepressant and taper more slowly; (3) fluoxetine has lowest risk and can be used as a bridge when switching antidepressants. Key exam distinction: discontinuation syndrome starts quickly (2-4 days), resolves with reintroduction; relapse takes 2+ weeks to develop.
source: BNF; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; NICE CG90

stem: A 48-year-old man presents with a 4-week history of elevated mood, increased energy, reduced need for sleep (sleeping 3 hours per night but feeling rested), grandiose plans to start multiple businesses, excessive spending, and rapid speech. He has had two previous similar episodes requiring hospital admission. He has no depressive episodes. He is currently not on any medication. His BMI is 32, fasting glucose is 6.8 mmol/L, and his wife reports he drinks heavily when well. What is the most appropriate first-line acute treatment for his current episode?
distractors_rationale: Lithium is effective for acute mania but has a slow onset of action (7-14 days) and requires pre-treatment bloods (U&Es, TFTs, pregnancy test) and monitoring. It is more commonly used as maintenance treatment. In acute mania, an antipsychotic is preferred for rapid symptom control.

Valproate is effective in acute mania but is now restricted in women of childbearing potential (MHRA 2024 warning). In this 48-year-old man, valproate is an option but not first-line. NICE recommends antipsychotics first for acute mania.

CORRECT. NICE CG185 recommends offering an antipsychotic (haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole) as first-line for acute mania. Olanzapine is a good choice here given rapid onset and evidence in mania (5-10mg daily, can be increased to 20mg). However, given his BMI is already elevated (32) and fasting glucose is impaired (6.8), olanzapine carries metabolic risk. An alternative antipsychotic with lower metabolic risk (e.g., aripiprazole) may be preferable, but olanzapine is the most commonly used first-line.

Aripiprazole is an effective antipsychotic for acute mania with lower metabolic risk than olanzapine. It would be a reasonable alternative but has a slower onset and can cause akathisia. Given that the question points towards 'most appropriate first-line', olanzapine is the standard answer.

Carbamazepine is reserved for treatment-resistant cases or specific situations (e.g., rapid cycling). It is not first-line due to tolerability, significant CYP450 induction (drug interactions), and need for monitoring. It also auto-induces its own metabolism.
teaching_point: Acute mania management (NICE CG185): First-line = antipsychotic (haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole). If the patient is already on a mood stabiliser, optimise the dose. Consider adding a short-term benzodiazepine (lorazepam) for agitation/insomnia. Lithium and valproate can be added but have slower onset. Key considerations: patient preference, previous response, side-effect profile (metabolic, EPS). Lithium and valproate are first-line for MAINTENANCE but not for acute control. NICE recommends continuing the antipsychotic for 3-6 months after remission.
source: NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder (updated); Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 800mg daily for 3 years. She presents at 8 weeks pregnant (confirmed by dating scan). She wants to know the safest option for her and the baby regarding mood stabiliser treatment. She has a history of two manic episodes, the last being 15 months ago. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Stop lithium immediately due to teratogenicity
Continue lithium at current dose with close monitoring
Continue lithium at a lower dose with dose adjustment and enhanced monitoring
distractors_rationale: Abruptly stopping lithium is dangerous. The risk of relapse in bipolar disorder during pregnancy is very high (especially postpartum). Lithium has been associated with Ebstein's anomaly (absolute risk 1-2/1000 with first-trimester exposure — RR ~3-5), but this risk is lower than previously thought and is dose-dependent. The risk of untreated bipolar relapse often outweighs the risks of lithium.

Continuing at the same dose is not ideal because physiological changes in pregnancy (increased GFR, expanded plasma volume) affect lithium levels. Lithium levels must be monitored more frequently and the dose may need to be adjusted to maintain therapeutic levels while minimising exposure.

Valproate is now ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy due to high teratogenicity (7-10% neural tube defects) and neurodevelopmental effects (30-40% risk of developmental delay, 42% IQ <80). The MHRA has introduced a pregnancy prevention programme for valproate. It must NOT be prescribed to any woman of childbearing potential unless criteria are met.

Lamotrigine is considered safer in pregnancy (lower teratogenicity ~2-3%) and is a good option for bipolar depression maintenance. However, switching to lamotrigine mid-pregnancy carries risk of destabilisation (washout + titration period). It may not be sufficient for prevention of manic episodes (stronger evidence for bipolar depression maintenance than mania prevention).

CORRECT. The recommended approach is to continue lithium at the lowest effective dose with dose adjustment as pregnancy progresses. Key steps: (1) discuss risks and benefits; (2) check baseline lithium level, U&Es, TFTs; (3) monitor lithium levels every 4 weeks (then weekly near term); (4) maintain level at lower end of therapeutic range (0.4-0.6 mmol/L); (5) avoid dehydration/hyperemesis; (6) at delivery, reduce dose to pre-pregnancy level and recheck within 1 week; (7) monitor neonate for lithium toxicity (hypotonia, cyanosis, bradycardia). Detailed foetal anomaly scan at 18-20 weeks recommended.
teaching_point: Lithium in pregnancy: The risk of Ebstein's anomaly with first-trimester lithium exposure is lower than previously thought (1-2/1000 vs earlier estimates of 1/20). Current guidelines (NICE CG192, BAP, Maudsley) recommend: (1) discuss risks of untreated bipolar disorder (relapse rate 50-90% if medication stopped) vs small risk of lithium; (2) if lithium is continued, use the lowest effective dose; (3) monitor serum levels 4-weekly; (4) detailed foetal anomaly scan; (5) avoid dehydration, NSAIDs, and diuretics. Valproate is contraindicated. Lamotrigine and some antipsychotics (quetiapine, olanzapine) are alternatives with better pregnancy safety profiles. Postpartum relapse risk is particularly high for bipolar women (30-50% in first 3 months).
source: NICE CG192: Antenatal and postnatal mental health; NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines 2024; BAP Guidelines

stem: A 55-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents with a 4-week history of low mood, anhedonia, poor concentration, and feelings of worthlessness. Six weeks ago, she was hospitalised for acute mania which was successfully treated with olanzapine 15mg daily. Her mood stabiliser is lithium (level 0.7 mmol/L, therapeutic). PHQ-9 is 18. She has no psychotic features and is medically well. What is the most appropriate management for her bipolar depression?
options: Increase lithium dose to achieve level 0.8-1.0 mmol/L
Add fluoxetine 20mg daily and continue olanzapine (OFC)
Add lamotrigine 25mg daily with slow titration
distractors_rationale: Lithine augmentation alone is unlikely to treat an acute bipolar depressive episode. While keeping lithium at the therapeutic range is important for maintenance, the depressive episode requires additional treatment.

Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar depression is controversial and generally NOT recommended by NICE. Antidepressants can precipitate manic switching, especially in bipolar I and without mood stabiliser cover. If an antidepressant is used, it must be combined with an antimanic agent (antipsychotic or mood stabiliser). SSRIs alone carry ~15-20% switch risk.
