stem: A 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder develops acute mania. She has a history of lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI). Which mood stabiliser is most appropriate for managing the NDI while continuing an effective antimanic agent?
options: Continue lithium and add amiloride 5mg BD
Stop lithium and start loop diuretic
distractors_rationale: CORRECT. Lithium-induced NDI occurs in 10-20% of patients. Lithium enters collecting duct cells via ENaC channels and inhibits aquaporin-2 expression. Amiloride blocks ENaC channels and reduces lithium entry, treating NDI while allowing lithium continuation. This is a useful strategy if lithium is otherwise effective.
Switching to carbamazepine is an option if NDI cannot be managed, but amiloride is first-line for NDI management.
Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic which can worsen NDI and cause electrolyte disturbance. Not appropriate.
Desmopressin (synthetic ADH) treats the symptom but not the cause. The kidney is ADH-resistant in NDI, so desmopressin will not be effective.
Loop diuretics can worsen electrolyte disturbance and are not indicated for NDI management.
teaching_point: Lithium-induced NDI: Mechanism: lithium inhibits GSK3-beta, reducing aquaporin-2 expression in collecting ducts. Presents with polydipsia and polyuria. Management: (1) Check lithium level; (2) Amiloride 5-10mg daily; (3) Reduce dose if safe; (4) Ensure hydration; (5) If severe, switch mood stabiliser. NDI is slowly reversible.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; BNF; Grunfeld JP et al. Lithium-induced NDI

stem: A 28-year-old woman with bipolar II disorder is currently euthymic. She has a history of three depressive episodes and two hypomanic episodes over 4 years. She is not pregnant and wishes to conceive next year. She wants to minimise medication in pregnancy. Which mood stabiliser is the safest option for maintenance in someone planning pregnancy?
distractors_rationale: Lithium carries risk of Ebstein anomaly (1-2/1000) and requires careful monitoring. It is not the safest option in pregnancy.
Valproate is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (MHRA pregnancy prevention programme) due to high neural tube defect risk (7-10%) and neurodevelopmental effects (42% IQ <80).

CORRECT. Lamotrigine is the safest mood stabiliser in pregnancy. The risk of major congenital malformations is approximately 2-3% (similar to background risk of 1-2%). It does not cause neural tube defects (unlike valproate and carbamazepine). Lamotrigine is particularly effective for preventing depressive episodes, which is relevant for bipolar II (where depression dominates). Levels of lamotrigine fall significantly in pregnancy (due to increased clearance) and must be monitored and adjusted. Bipolar II: lamotrigine first-line for maintenance (NICE CG185).
Carbamazepine carries increased risk of neural tube defects (0.5-1%) and requires folic acid 5mg. It is not the safest option.

Quetiapine is relatively safe in pregnancy (antipsychotic, not a classical mood stabiliser) but carries metabolic risk. It is effective for both depression and mania but lamotrigine has a better safety profile in pregnancy.
teaching_point: Lamotrigine in pregnancy: (1) Lowest teratogenic risk among mood stabilisers; (2) Levels drop by 50% in pregnancy due to increased glucuronidation — monitor levels and increase dose; (3) Levels rise back postpartum — reduce dose within 48 hours to avoid toxicity; (4) Folic acid 5mg recommended; (5) Neonatal monitoring for withdrawal/toxicity. Valproate is now essentially contraindicated in any woman of childbearing potential without a pregnancy prevention programme. Bipolar II maintenance: NICE recommends lamotrigine as first-line (stronger evidence for depression prophylaxis). Lithium is first-line for bipolar I.
source: NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder; NICE CG192: Perinatal mental health; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 55-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium for 15 years. His latest U&Es show eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m2 (down from 62 one year ago). His lithium level is 0.6 mmol/L (therapeutic). He has no proteinuria and normal urine output. His blood pressure is 136/84. He is on no nephrotoxic medications. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop lithium immediately and switch to valproate
Reduce lithium dose to achieve level 0.4-0.5 mmol/L and refer to nephrology
Continue lithium at the same dose as eGFR >30 is acceptable
Add an ACE inhibitor to reduce proteinuria
Switch lithium to lamotrigine and start quetiapine
distractors_rationale: Stopping lithium abruptly is dangerous (relapse risk) and not indicated unless eGFR <15-20 or rapidly declining despite optimisation.

CORRECT. Lithium-induced renal impairment: a decline in eGFR >20% from baseline or rate of decline >5 mL/min/year warrants intervention. This patient's eGFR dropped from 62 to 48 in 1 year (decline of 14 — >5/year). Management: (1) Reduce lithium to lowest effective level (0.4-0.5 mmol/L for maintenance); (2) Refer to nephrology for further assessment; (3) Monitor U&Es 3-monthly; (4) Avoid NSAIDs, dehydration, ACE inhibitors; (5) If eGFR continues to decline despite optimisation, consider switching mood stabiliser.
An eGFR decline to <60 with a significant drop over 1 year requires action. 'eGFR >30 is acceptable' would be under-responding to a significant decline.

ACE inhibitors are part of general renal protection but carry risk of increasing lithium toxicity (reduce GFR, can increase lithium levels). They should only be prescribed with extreme caution in lithium patients.
Switching to lamotrigine + quetiapine is premature at this stage. The first step is dose optimisation and nephrology review.
teaching_point: Lithium and renal impairment: Chronic lithium therapy causes tubulointerstitial nephropathy and reduced GFR. Monitoring: U&Es/eGFR every 6 months. Action thresholds: eGFR decline >20% from baseline, or rapid decline >5 mL/min/year, or eGFR <30. Management: (1) Lowers dose level (target 0.4-0.5); (2) Nephrology referral; (3) Avoid NSAIDs; (4) Monitor 3-monthly; (5) If eGFR <30 or continuing decline, consider switching to valproate or lamotrigine. Lithium is NOT nephrotoxic at standard doses in most patients — the risk is chronic. The annual eGFR decline on lithium is approximately 0-2 mL/min/year (vs 0-1 for the general population). Acute kidney injury can occur with toxicity. NICE CG185: monitor U&Es and eGFR every 6 months.
source: NICE CG185; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; BNF

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with depressed mood, anhedonia, low energy, and hypersomnia. She reports that her 'limbs feel like lead' and she is highly sensitive to perceived rejection. She has no history of mania or hypomania. Her PHQ-9 is 18. There is a family history of bipolar disorder in her father. Her depression has not responded to sequential trials of sertraline (50mg for 8 weeks) and mirtazapine (30mg for 6 weeks). What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start quetiapine 150mg nocte and reassess the possibility of bipolar depression
distractors_rationale: Aripiprazole augmentation is a NICE-recommended strategy for treatment-resistant unipolar depression. However, this patient's clinical features (hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity — atypical depression features) and family history of bipolar disorder should raise suspicion for bipolar depression.

Switching to another antidepressant (SNRI) after two SSRI/NaSSA failures is an option for unipolar TRD, but the clinical picture (atypical features, family history, poor response to antidepressants) should prompt consideration of bipolarity.

CORRECT. This patient has several 'bipolar flags': (1) Atypical depressive features (hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity); (2) Family history of bipolar disorder; (3) Poor response to two antidepressant monotherapies (antidepressants can be ineffective or destabilising in bipolar depression). Quetiapine is first-line for bipolar depression (NICE CG185) and would be the appropriate choice if bipolar II is suspected. She should be reassessed carefully for hypomanic episodes using collateral history and the HCL-32 or MDQ. Bipolar II is often misdiagnosed as unipolar depression.

Lamotrigine is for bipolar maintenance (especially depression prophylaxis), not acute treatment. It is too slow (takes 6-8 weeks to reach therapeutic dose) and would not be appropriate as monotherapy for acute depression where bipolar depression is suspected.
ECT is not indicated at this stage — the patient has moderate depression without psychotic features, catatonia, or acute risk.
teaching_point: Recognising bipolar depression vs unipolar depression: Bipolar depression is more likely if: (1) Atypical features (hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis); (2) Early onset (<25 years); (3) Postpartum depression; (4) Antidepressant-induced mania/hypomania; (5) Poor response to antidepressant monotherapy; (6) Family history of bipolar disorder; (7) Cyclothymic temperament; (8) More frequent episodes. The HCL-32 (Hypomania Checklist) and MDQ (Mood Disorder Questionnaire) are screening tools. Treatment: first-line = quetiapine; alternatives = olanzapine, lamotrigine (maintenance). Antidepressants should only be used with mood stabiliser cover.
source: NICE CG185; DSM-5-TR; HCL-32 screening tool

stem: A 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents with her third manic episode in 2 years. She is currently on lithium (level 0.5 mmol/L) and takes it erratically. She finds the side effects of lithium unpleasant (tremor, polydipsia) and is not motivated to improve adherence. Her BMI is 28. She is not pregnant. What is the most appropriate maintenance strategy?
options: Increase lithium dose and counsel about adherence
Switch to a long-acting injectable antipsychotic (aripiprazole LAI)
Continue lithium and add quetiapine 150mg nocte augmentation
distractors_rationale: Further increasing lithium dose is unlikely to help if the patient is poorly adherent due to side effects. A different approach is needed.

Valproate is effective for maintenance, especially in women with poor adherence, but is now strictly restricted in women of childbearing potential due to MHRA warnings. At 32, she is in this age group. Valproate requires adherence counselling and a pregnancy prevention programme. It also carries weight gain risk (her BMI is 28).

CORRECT. This patient is a good candidate for a LAI antipsychotic because: (1) She has recurrent manic episodes despite lithium — she may benefit from a different maintenance strategy; (2) She is poorly adherent with oral medication — LAI ensures consistent delivery; (3) Aripiprazole LAI has a low metabolic side effect profile (important given BMI 28) and is weight-neutral; (4) It is licensed for maintenance in bipolar I. Aripiprazole LAI 400mg monthly is effective for preventing manic relapse. NICE CG185 recommends LAIs for maintenance when adherence is a concern. Other options: olanzapine LAI, risperidone LAI (but prolactin risk) or paliperidone LAI.
Lamotrigine monotherapy is not recommended for maintenance in bipolar I (evidence stronger for depression than mania prevention). It also requires slow titration.

Lithium + quetiapine augmentation is a valid option, but if adherence is the core issue (she takes lithium erratically), adding another oral medication won't address it. A depot/LAI addresses adherence directly.
teaching_point: LAIs in bipolar disorder: Indications: (1) Poor adherence with oral medication; (2) Patient preference (convenience); (3) Chronic recurrent illness. LAI options for bipolar: aripiprazole LAI (monthly — best metabolic profile, prevents mania), olanzapine LAI (PDSS risk, metabolic concerns), risperidone LAI (prolactin elevation, weight gain). NICE advises: 'Consider a depot/LAI antipsychotic for people with bipolar disorder who would prefer it, or for those who have poor adherence with oral medication and have relapsed as a result.' Valproate restrictions: in women of childbearing potential, must have a pregnancy prevention programme. The patient is 32 and not pregnant but still within childbearing age.
source: NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 48-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents with a mixed affective episode — she is depressed, tearful, and hopeless but also irritable, easily distracted, and full of energy. She has had poor sleep for 4-5 days. She is not currently on medication. What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?
options: Sertraline 50mg daily to target depressive symptoms
distractors_rationale: Antidepressants in mixed affective states are generally not recommended by NICE. They can worsen the manic component of the mixed episode and carry risk of accelerating cycling or inducing mania.
Lithium has evidence in acute mania but has a slow onset (7-14 days) and requires pre-treatment bloods. In acute mixed episodes, first-line is an antipsychotic.
Valproate is effective in mixed episodes (has some evidence for mixed states) but is not first-line in NICE CG185. An antipsychotic is preferred.

CORRECT. NICE CG185 recommends an antipsychotic (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, haloperidol, aripiprazole) as first-line for acute mixed episodes. Olanzapine 5-10mg has evidence for mixed episodes (both manic and depressive symptoms). When the patient stabilises, consider starting a mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate) for maintenance. Olanzapine is rapidly effective (within 2-4 days) for manic symptoms and has some effect on depressive symptoms in mixed states.
Lamotrigine is not effective for acute mixed episodes. It is a MAINTENANCE treatment for bipolar depression prophylaxis. It is too slow (6-8 weeks titration) for acute treatment.
teaching_point: Mixed affective episode: Defined in DSM-5-TR as a manic episode with at least 3 depressive symptoms (dysphoric mania) OR a depressive episode with at least 3 manic symptoms (mixed episode). ICD-11 also recognises mixed episodes. Key management principles: (1) Antipsychotics first-line (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone); (2) Avoid antidepressants (can worsen the episode); (3) After stabilisation, consider mood stabiliser for maintenance; (4) Valproate has some evidence for mixed states; (5) Lithium is effective but slower. Differential: rapid cycling (4+ episodes/yr, each discrete), mixed episode (simultaneous manic and depressive symptoms). Mixed episodes are associated with higher suicide risk and poorer treatment response.
source: NICE CG185; DSM-5-TR; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 40-year-old man with bipolar I disorder and mild learning disability is being started on lithium for maintenance. He lives in supported accommodation. He is on no other medication. What is the most important lithium monitoring requirement before starting?
options: U&Es, TFTs, serum calcium, pregnancy test, and weight
distractors_rationale: ECG is recommended before starting lithium if the patient has cardiac risk factors or is >50 years, but is not mandatory for all.

CORRECT. NICE CG185 and the BNF require BEFORE starting lithium: (1) U&Es (to ensure normal renal function); (2) TFTs (thyroid abnormalities common with lithium); (3) Serum calcium (lithium can cause hyperparathyroidism); (4) Pregnancy test for women of childbearing potential; (5) Weight/BMI (baseline for metabolic monitoring). THEN check lithium level 5-7 days after each dose change until therapeutic. Then lithium levels every 3 months, and U&Es/TFTs/Ca every 6 months. In this patient with learning disability, it is particularly important to have a clear monitoring plan and involve carers/support workers.
FBC and LFTs are not a standard requirement for lithium initiation but may be checked as part of routine health screening.
Chest X-ray is not required for lithium.
Only checking lithium levels is insufficient — baseline renal and thyroid function are essential to establish a reference point before starting.
teaching_point: Lithium pre-treatment checks — must-do: (1) U&Es and eGFR (baseline renal function); (2) TFTs (TSH, fT4); (3) Serum calcium (lithium can cause hyperparathyroidism); (4) Weight and BMI; (5) Pregnancy test (if applicable); (6) ECG (if >50 or cardiovascular risk). Ongoing monitoring: lithium level every 3 months (12-hour post-dose trough). U&Es, TFTs, Ca every 6 months. Weight, BMI, HbA1c, lipids annually. Lithium interacts with: NSAIDs (increase levels), thiazide diuretics (increase levels), ACE inhibitors (increase levels), metronidazole (increase levels). Lithium level targets: acute mania 0.6-1.0, maintenance 0.4-0.8. Elderly: 0.4-0.6.
source: BNF; NICE CG185; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 35-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is euthymic on quetiapine 300mg nocte. She has a history of two manic episodes and one depressive episode. She wants to discuss long-term treatment. She is concerned about weight gain (5kg over 1 year) and sedation. Her BMI is 27. What is the most appropriate maintenance strategy according to NICE?
options: Continue quetiapine as it is effective for both mania and depression
Switch to lithium as first-line maintenance and offer lifestyle advice for weight
Add lamotrigine to allow quetiapine dose reduction
Taper and stop quetiapine after 2 years of stability
distractors_rationale: While quetiapine is effective for bipolar maintenance, it is not first-line maintenance. NICE recommends lithium as first-line maintenance for bipolar I. If there are tolerability issues (weight gain, sedation), a switch to first-line treatment should be discussed.

CORRECT. NICE CG185 recommends: 'Offer lithium as first-line maintenance treatment for bipolar disorder.' Lithium has the strongest evidence for preventing both manic and depressive relapses and is the only medication with proven suicide prevention effect. For patients concerned about weight gain and sedation (common with quetiapine), switching to lithium is appropriate. Lithium is weight-neutral and does not cause sedation. Lifestyle advice for weight should accompany any medication changes.

Adding lamotrigine to quetiapine is a valid augmentation strategy, but if the patient is having significant tolerability issues with quetiapine, switching to a simpler first-line option (lithium) is preferable to polypharmacy.

Valproate is not first-line for maintenance (lithium is). In a woman of childbearing potential (35 years), valproate is now strictly restricted (MHRA pregnancy prevention programme). It also carries weight gain risk similar to quetiapine.
NICE recommends at least 2-5 years of maintenance after a manic episode (often lifelong). Given she has had 2 manic + 1 depressive episode, long-term treatment is indicated.
teaching_point: Maintenance treatment for bipolar I: First-line: lithium (strongest evidence for mania and depression prevention + suicide reduction). Alternatives if lithium is not tolerated or ineffective: (1) Valproate (but restricted in women of childbearing potential); (2) Olanzapine (metabolic risk); (3) Quetiapine (sedation, metabolic); (4) Aripiprazole LAI; (5) Lamotrigine (adjunctive, especially for depression prevention). Duration: at least 2-5 years after a manic episode, often lifelong. NICE: 'Continue maintenance treatment for at least 2 years after a manic episode and for longer if there are risk factors for relapse (e.g., frequent episodes, severe episodes, poor insight, substance misuse).' Lithium monitoring must continue for the duration of treatment.
source: NICE CG185; BNF; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 30-year-old man with bipolar I disorder is admitted to a psychiatric unit with acute mania for the third time in 18 months. He was previously on lithium 800mg (level 0.6 mmol/L) but discontinued it 6 months ago due to 'feeling fine'. He is now agitated, grandiose, and refusing all oral medication. His ECG shows QTc 460ms. Observations: BP 138/86, HR 105, Temp 36.8°C. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Haloperidol 10mg IM (higher dose for rapid effect)
distractors_rationale: IM olanzapine is effective but carries risk of post-injection syndrome and excessive sedation. Also, the QTc of 460ms warrants caution — olanzapine is relatively QTc-neutral. The combination of haloperidol + lorazepam is the standard first-line for rapid tranquillisation.

CORRECT. For rapid tranquillisation of an agitated/aggressive patient with acute mania, NICE recommends IM haloperidol (5mg) plus IM lorazepam (2mg). This is the most studied and recommended combination. Haloperidol is a high-potency antipsychotic with rapid onset by IM route. Lorazepam adds sedation and reduces the antipsychotic dose needed. QTc 460ms is borderline but acceptable for haloperidol IM (caution at higher doses).
Haloperidol 10mg is a higher dose which may increase EPS and QTc risk unnecessarily. The recommended dose is 5mg, with 2mg lorazepam.
Aripiprazole orally is not appropriate — the patient is refusing oral medication and needs rapid, reliable administration.
Quetiapine orally is not appropriate for the same reason. It also has a slower onset than haloperidol IM.
teaching_point: Rapid tranquillisation in acute mania: First-line IM: haloperidol 5mg + lorazepam 2mg IM (NICE CG10, NICE CG185). Alternative if QTc is borderline or prolonged: consider IM lorazepam alone and IM antipsychotic with caution. Rapid tranquillisation guidelines: (1) De-escalation first; (2) Offer oral medication if possible; (3) If refused, IM haloperidol + lorazepam; (4) Monitor QTc before repeat doses; (5) Avoid IM clozapine + IM benzodiazepine (respiratory depression risk). After the acute episode, discuss maintenance treatment. NICE: patients with 2+ manic episodes in 12 months should be offered lithium maintenance.
source: NICE CG10: Violence and aggression; NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 41-year-old man with treatment-resistant depression (failed 3 antidepressants) and no history of mania/hypomania is referred for a second opinion. On careful chart review and collateral from his wife, he has had three episodes lasting 2-3 days of elevated mood, grandiosity, reduced need for sleep, and increased goal-directed activity. These were not impairing. His depressive episodes are severe and frequent. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?
options: Unipolar depression with cyclothymic temperament — continue antidepressant treatment
Bipolar II disorder — start quetiapine 150-300mg nocte and taper antidepressants
distractors_rationale: This patient has hypomanic episodes (clear discrete episodes with elevated mood, grandiosity, reduced need for sleep) — this rules out unipolar depression. Bipolar II is defined by hypomania + major depression. The 2-3 day episodes are borderline brief (<4 days required by DSM-5-TR), but ICD-11 is more flexible. Clinically, if they are clearly hypomanic in phenotype, bipolar II is the working diagnosis.

CORRECT. Bipolar II disorder: one or more hypomanic episodes + at least one major depressive episode. No history of mania. This patient meets criteria. Treatment: quetiapine first-line (NICE CG185). Antidepressants should be tapered (they may worsen cycling in bipolar II). He failed 3 antidepressant trials — this should have prompted screening for bipolarity earlier. HCL-32 and MDQ screening are crucial in TRD.
Bipolar I requires a full manic episode (≥1 week, or less if hospitalised, with marked functional impairment or psychotic features). This patient has never been manic — only hypomanic.
Schizoaffective disorder requires psychotic symptoms in the absence of mood episodes. This patient's elevated mood and depression are mood episodes without psychosis.
Cyclothymia requires chronic fluctuating mood disturbance without discrete episodes meeting hypomania or major depression criteria. This patient has clear depressive episodes meeting criteria.
teaching_point: Bipolar II is a critical diagnosis to catch in TRD. Prevalence: 10-20% of TRD patients have unrecognised bipolar II. Screening tools: HCL-32 >14, MDQ >7. Key clinical features: (1) Early onset <25; (2) Atypical depression (hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity); (3) Postpartum depression; (4) Antidepressant 'poop-out' (loss of efficacy); (5) Antidepressant-induced switching/cycling; (6) Family history of bipolar; (7) 3+ antidepressant failures. Treatment: quetiapine first-line for bipolar depression (NICE). Alternative: lamotrigine for prophylaxis, olanzapine for acute depression. NEVER use antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar II.
source: NICE CG185; DSM-5-TR; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 44-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 800mg (level 0.6) and aripiprazole 15mg daily for 2 years. He develops new-onset hypertension (BP 152/94) and his GP wants to start an antihypertensive. Which antihypertensive is safest to use with lithium?
distractors_rationale: Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, bendroflumethiazide) reduce renal clearance of lithium by increasing proximal tubular reabsorption, potentially causing lithium toxicity. They should be avoided or used with extreme caution.
ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril) reduce GFR and can cause lithium retention and toxicity. They should be avoided if possible.

CORRECT. Amlodipine (calcium channel blocker) has no significant interaction with lithium. It does not affect renal function or lithium clearance. It is the safest antihypertensive to use with lithium. Other safe options: beta-blockers (e.g., bisoprolol) and potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g., amiloride — which treats lithium-induced NDI).

ARBs (losartan, candesartan) act on the renin-angiotensin system, similar to ACE inhibitors, and can reduce GFR. They carry a similar risk of lithium elevation, though the interaction is less well-studied than for ACE inhibitors. Best avoided.
See A — bendroflumethiazide is a thiazide diuretic with significant interaction.
teaching_point: Lithium and antihypertensives: AVOID: thiazide diuretics (lithium toxicity by increased reabsorption), ACE inhibitors (lithium toxicity by reduced GFR). USE WITH CAUTION: ARBs (similar mechanism to ACE inhibitors but less significant — still monitor lithium levels). SAFE: Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine, verapamil/diltiazem — note verapamil may have mood effects), beta-blockers (bisoprolol, propranolol), potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride — beneficial for NDI). SAFEST: Amlodipine. Any new antihypertensive requires lithium level monitoring within 1 week of starting and every 3 months thereafter.
source: BNF; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is 6 weeks postpartum. She was stable on quetiapine 300mg throughout pregnancy. She presents with a 3-day history of rapidly worsening confusion, agitation, bizarre behaviour, and auditory hallucinations. She has slept very little in 72 hours and is refusing food. Temperature 37.6°C, HR 112, BP 138/88. She is breastfeeding. What is the most likely diagnosis and best management?
options: Postpartum depression with psychosis — admit to mother and baby unit, increase quetiapine to 600mg, consider ECT
Puerperal psychosis — admit to mother and baby unit, start antipsychotic (olanzapine or haloperidol), assess for lithium or ECT
Postpartum anxiety with insomnia — benzodiazepine and outpatient follow-up
Delirium due to infection — medical admission for investigations
distractors_rationale: Postpartum depression with psychosis is a recognised entity but is usually described as part of the puerperal psychosis spectrum. The rapid onset (hours to days), confusion, bizarre behaviour, and sleep loss are classic for puerperal psychosis.

CORRECT. Puerperal (postpartum) psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with onset typically within the first 2 weeks (but can occur up to 12 weeks). Features: rapid onset of psychotic symptoms, mood lability (usually manic or mixed), confusion, disorganised behaviour, sleep loss. Incidence: 1-2/1000 deliveries. Risk: 50% in bipolar women (if history of postpartum psychosis, risk 50-90%). Management: (1) URGENT admission to a specialist mother and baby unit (MBU); (2) Antipsychotic (olanzapine, haloperidol) — quetiapine dose can be increased; (3) Consider lithium augmentation (can be used in breastfeeding with monitoring); (4) ECT if severe/refractory; (5) Risk assessment (infanticide risk — 5% of cases involve infanticide, usually in the context of psychosis); (6) Assess breastfeeding — most antipsychotics at low levels in breastmilk; benefits usually outweigh risks.
The patient has psychotic symptoms — this is not anxiety/insomnia.

Delirium is in the differential but less likely given the history of bipolar and the classic presentation of puerperal psychosis. The absence of a clear medical cause (no fever, no medications known to cause delirium) makes puerperal psychosis more likely.
Postpartum blues affects 50-90% of women, peaks at day 3-5, resolves spontaneously within 2 weeks. It does NOT involve psychotic symptoms or such significant functional impairment.
teaching_point: Puerperal psychosis: HIGH-YIELD MRCPsych topic. Key facts: (1) Incidence 1-2/1000; (2) Onset 2-14 days postpartum (can be up to 12 weeks); (3) Risk factors: bipolar disorder (50% risk), previous puerperal psychosis (50-90% risk), family history of puerperal psychosis, primiparity, mode of delivery (Caesarean); (4) Features: mood symptoms (usually manic or mixed), psychotic symptoms (paranoid, grandiose, sometimes bizarre), confusion, disorganised behaviour, rapid onset; (5) Treatment: MBU admission, antipsychotics, lithium, ECT; (6) Prognosis: good — 90% recover fully; (7) Recurrence risk: 50% in subsequent pregnancies; (8) Infanticide risk: ~5% (usually via extended suicide). The Mental Health Act may be needed if the patient lacks capacity.
source: NICE CG192: Antenatal and postnatal mental health; NICE CG185; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 25-year-old man with bipolar I disorder presents with severe depression (PHQ-9 23) with psychotic features (nihilistic delusions, guilt). He has not responded to quetiapine 300mg nocte for 8 weeks. He refused augmentation with an antidepressant. His BMI is 22 and he has no medical problems. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Add lamotrigine 25mg daily with slow titration
distractors_rationale: Lamotrigine is for maintenance prophylaxis, not acute bipolar depression (especially with psychosis). It is too slow to titrate.

Increasing quetiapine is an option but only up to 400mg for bipolar depression. At 600mg, the evidence is for mania, not depression. The presence of psychotic features and severe functional impairment (PHQ-9 23) warrants a more urgent intervention.

OFC (olanzapine-fluoxetine combination) is an option for bipolar depression, but this patient has psychotic depression with severe symptoms. ECT has the highest evidence for psychotic depression (80-90% response). OFC would be slower.

CORRECT. ECT is first-line for severe depression with psychotic features (delusional depression) that has not responded to medication. In bipolar depression specifically, ECT is indicated when: (1) there is a high suicide risk; (2) psychotic features are present; (3) catatonia is present; (4) treatment resistance is evident (failed quetiapine, refused antidepressant augmentation). ECT has a response rate of 80-90% in psychotic depression. It is safe in bipolar disorder. The patient will need concurrent medication for maintenance after ECT.
Lithium augmentation is an option for bipolar depression but is slower (2-4 weeks to reach therapeutic levels) and less effective than ECT in psychotic depression.
teaching_point: ECT in bipolar depression: Indications: (1) Severe depression with psychotic features; (2) Treatment-resistant depression; (3) High suicide risk; (4) Catatonia; (5) Rapid response needed (e.g., poor food/fluid intake). ECT works faster than medication (usually within 2-4 sessions). In bipolar depression, ECT is effective for both mood and psychotic symptoms. Maintenance ECT can be considered for recurrent episodes. Cognitive side effects: anterograde amnesia (transient), retrograde amnesia (may persist). Right unilateral ECT has fewer cognitive side effects than bitemporal but is less effective. NICE TA136: ECT is recommended for severe depression, catatonia, and prolonged/severe mania.
source: NICE TA136: ECT; NICE CG185; NICE CG90

stem: A 38-year-old man with bipolar I disorder is on maintenance lithium (level 0.6 mmol/L). He wishes to start a weight-training programme and asks about creatine supplementation. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Creatine is safe and may help with antidepressant augmentation
Creatine can increase the risk of lithium toxicity through dehydration and reduced GFR — advise against it
Creatine is fine as long as he stays hydrated
Creatine does not interact with lithium at all
Creatine should be taken with NSAIDs to maximise absorption
distractors_rationale: Creatine does not have evidence for antidepressant augmentation, and there are safety concerns with lithium.

CORRECT. Creatine supplementation can cause: (1) Dehydration (creatine pulls water into muscles); (2) Increased creatinine (false reading — does not directly affect lithium clearance but reduced hydration can reduce GFR); (3) Potential renal stress in combination with lithium (both can affect renal function). The combination is not absolutely contraindicated but requires precautions: maintain excellent hydration, monitor U&Es/lithium levels closely, avoid over-supplementation. The safest advice is to avoid it on lithium.
Even with adequate hydration, creatine can cause renal stress and should be used with caution on lithium.
There is a potential interaction via hydration status.
NSAIDs should never be taken with lithium (they reduce lithium clearance and can cause acute toxicity).
teaching_point: Exercise and lithium: Strenuous exercise can cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, potentially affecting lithium levels. Patients on lithium should: (1) Maintain adequate hydration (especially during exercise); (2) Be aware of signs of lithium toxicity (nausea, tremor, ataxia); (3) Avoid supplements that may affect renal function or hydration; (4) Monitor weight and metabolic health (exercise is beneficial). Creatine specifically: draws water into muscle cells, increasing fluid requirements. On lithium, this creates a risk of relative dehydration and reduced GFR → increased lithium levels. If the patient chooses to use creatine: strict hydration, monitor U&Es and lithium levels 2 weeks after starting.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; BNF

stem: A 60-year-old man with bipolar I disorder presents with acute mania. He has a history of myocardial infarction 6 months ago, is on bisoprolol 5mg, atorvastatin 40mg, and aspirin 75mg. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 465ms. What is the most appropriate antimanic agent?
distractors_rationale: Haloperidol carries significant QTc prolongation risk (especially in elderly/those with cardiac history). QTc of 465ms is borderline — haloperidol could worsen this. Also carries EPS risk in an elderly patient.

Lithium has a slow onset (7-14 days) and requires pre-treatment bloods (U&Es, TFTs). It is not ideal for acute management and carries cardiac risks (lithium can cause T-wave changes and rarely arrhythmias). The patient is on aspirin and atorvastatin — no direct interaction but lithium levels need monitoring.

Valproate is effective for acute mania, but carries weight gain and metabolic risk. It also causes thrombocytopenia (potential issue with aspirin). It is an option but not the safest given his QTc and metabolic profile.

CORRECT. Olanzapine is the best choice here because: (1) It has minimal QTc prolongation (safe with his prolonged QTc); (2) Effective for acute mania with rapid onset (2-4 days); (3) No significant interaction with cardiac medications; (4) Can be given IM if needed; (5) Safe post-MI (no negative inotropic effects, no significant QTc effect). The metabolic effects of olanzapine are a concern (weight, lipids) but for acute management in a patient with cardiac disease, QTc safety outweighs this. Metabolic monitoring should continue long-term.
Carbamazepine has significant CYP450 induction (interacts with atorvastatin, bisoprolol), carries blood dyscrasias risk, and is not first-line. It also has QTc effects.
teaching_point: Antimanic choice in cardiac patients: Olanzapine is the safest in terms of QTc profile and cardiac safety. Risperidone is also relatively QTc-safe but has prolactin risk. Quetiapine has moderate QTc effect. Haloperidol has the highest QTc risk (especially IM). Lithium is effective for maintenance but slow for acute; can cause ECG changes (T-wave inversion, U waves). Valproate is an option but carries metabolic risk. Carbamazepine has significant drug interactions (CYP induction). Key principle: in patients with pre-existing QTc prolongation or cardiac disease, choose an antipsychotic with minimal QTc effect (olanzapine, aripiprazole). Monitor ECG regularly.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; BNF; NICE CG185

stem: A 22-year-old university student presents to student health with low mood, anhedonia, poor concentration, and difficulty falling asleep (initial insomnia) for 4 weeks. She also reports periods of feeling 'empty' and intense anger triggered by perceived rejection from her boyfriend. She has used alcohol and cannabis to cope. She has a history of self-harm (cutting) at age 16-17. She describes chronic feelings of emptiness and unclear self-image. PHQ-9 is 15. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed
Borderline personality disorder with comorbid depression
distractors_rationale: While she has depressive symptoms (meeting criteria for MDD), the additional features (chronic emptiness, identity disturbance, intense anger at rejection, history of self-harm, mood instability triggered by interpersonal stress) suggest the depression is occurring in the context of BPD. The core issue is BPD, not unipolar depression.

There is no history of discrete hypomanic episodes. The mood swings in BPD are triggered by interpersonal stress, not spontaneous hypomania. The chronic emptiness and identity disturbance are not features of bipolar II.

CORRECT. This patient meets DSM-5-TR criteria for borderline personality disorder with a comorbid depressive episode. BPD features: (1) Chronic emptiness; (2) Identity disturbance; (3) Affective instability due to reactivity of mood; (4) Intense anger/difficulty controlling anger; (5) Transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation; (6) History of self-harm; (7) Frantic efforts to avoid abandonment. The depressive episode should be treated according to NICE guidelines — but with caution: antidepressants in BPD have limited evidence and NICE does not recommend them for BPD per se.

Cyclothymia requires chronic hypomanic and depressive symptoms that do not meet full episode criteria. This patient has BPD symptoms (identity disturbance, chronic emptiness, self-harm history) that are not explained by cyclothymia.
Adjustment disorder requires a clear stressor within the previous 3 months. The symptoms here are more chronic and pervasive, consistent with a personality disorder.
teaching_point: BPD vs bipolar II vs depression — a common MRCPsych differential: BPD key features: (1) Affective instability is brief (hours to days), triggered by interpersonal stress; (2) Chronic emptiness vs episodic low mood; (3) Identity disturbance, chronic; (4) Self-harm is often for emotional regulation. Bipolar II: (1) Episodic hypomania (≥4 days); (2) Episodic depression; (3) Mood episodes are spontaneous; (4) Self-harm less common. NICE CG78 for BPD: 'Do not use drug treatment specifically for BPD or for individual symptoms or behaviour associated with BPD.' Antidepressants should not be used first-line for depression in BPD unless there is a clear major depressive episode of significant duration and severity.
source: NICE CG78: Borderline personality disorder; NICE CG90; DSM-5-TR
